title: The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places
authors: Byron Reeves, Clifford Nass
summary: Canonical experimental demonstration that people automatically apply social rules to computers and media as real social actors; the foundational mechanism making the 'AI Pet' mental model instantly available to players without instruction.

title: Disposable Love: The Rise and Fall of a Virtual Pet
authors: Linda-Renée Bloch, Dafna Lemish
summary: Early cultural analysis of the Tamagotchi as a nurturing-relationship artifact; documents the original 'Tamagotchi effect' phenomenon the Pet scale builds on.

title: Hardware Companions? What Online AIBO Discussion Forums Reveal about the Human-Robotic Relationship
authors: Batya Friedman, Peter H. Kahn Jr., Jennifer Hagman
summary: Analysis of 6,000+ AIBO forum posts showing adults attribute mental states and rapport to a robot pet while knowing it is a machine — the dual-stance 'alive enough' attachment C1 assumes as the player's starting model.

title: Living With Seal Robots — Its Sociopsychological and Physiological Influences on the Elderly at a Care House
authors: Kazuyoshi Wada, Takanori Shibata
summary: Longitudinal Paro study showing increased social interaction and improved physiological stress markers in elder care; strongest evidence that attachment to artificial companions has measurable real effects, grounding the seriousness of the Pet scale.

title: Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other
authors: Sherry Turkle
summary: Canonical account of the 'robotic moment' and taking sociable technology 'at interface value'; Turkle's critique names precisely the naive attachment stance the paper's progression is designed to move players beyond.

title: My Chatbot Companion - a Study of Human-Chatbot Relationships
authors: Marita Skjuve, Asbjørn Følstad, Knut Inge Fostervold, Petter Bae Brandtzaeg
summary: Interview study of 18 Replika users showing human-chatbot relationships evolve through self-disclosure to stable affective bonds — the contemporary form of the Pet-scale mental model C1 starts from.

title: Loneliness and Suicide Mitigation for Students Using GPT3-Enabled Chatbots
authors: Bethanie Maples, Merve Cerit, Aditya Vishwanath, Roy Pea
summary: Survey of 1,006 student Replika users finding high loneliness alongside perceived support; shows current stakes of unexamined attachment to LLM companions, supporting the motivation that agent literacy must start where users actually are — at attachment.

title: Animal Companions: Fostering Children's Effort-Making by Nurturing Virtual Pets
authors: Zhi-Hong Chen, Chih-Yueh Chou, Yi-Chan Deng, Tak-Wai Chan
summary: The My-Pet line harnesses children's emotional attachment to a nurtured virtual pet as a motivational scaffold with experimental evidence. Direct novelty threat to C1: pet attachment as pedagogical on-ramp is established prior art; differentiation must be by target concept (agent literacy, progression away from the pet).

title: Pet-Like Learning Companions: Past Research and Future Directions
authors: Zhi-Hong Chen, Hsiu-Ling Hsu, Chiu-Fan Huang, Chen-Yu Liao, Chih-Yueh Chou
venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 20, article 033
summary: Review of two decades of pet-like learning companions including their generative-AI future; sharpens the novelty threat to C1, but the reviewed learning content is curricular subjects, not literacy about AI agents themselves — the differentiation seam.

title: Purr-ogrammed Love: A Narrative Review of Virtual Pets
authors: Michaela Dodd, Allan Fowler, Danielle Lottridge
summary: Narrative review of 45 virtual-pet articles (six themes); the field's current map, notably surfacing no prior work using pets to teach agentic-AI concepts specifically.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
authors: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein
venue: UIST '23 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
summary: [MERGED: found independently by two searchers] Smallville: 25 LLM agents with memory/reflection/planning form relationships and coordinate in a Sims-like sandbox — the canonical believable 'AI village' and closest prior art to a playable one. It frames no governance seam between generative output and world mutation and is a believability research artifact whose agents freely mutate the world, not a pedagogy in a scaled progression.

title: The Role of Emotion in Believable Agents
authors: Joseph Bates
venue: Communications of the ACM 37(7), CMU Oz Project
summary: Founding statement of the believable-agents lineage: the artistic 'illusion of life' matters more than rational competence; anchors the Pet attachment scale in a three-decade tradition.

title: Human-Level AI's Killer Application: Interactive Computer Games
authors: John E. Laird, Michael van Lent
summary: Classic argument that games are the ideal testbed for human-level AI; legitimizes using a playable game as the vehicle for engaging with agentic AI.

title: Large Language Models and Games: A Survey and Roadmap
authors: Roberto Gallotta, Graham Todd, Marvin Zammit, Sam Earle, Antonios Liapis, Julian Togelius, Georgios N. Yannakakis
summary: First comprehensive survey of LLM roles in games; its taxonomy shows 'LLM as NPC' is well-trodden but a governance-first sovereign-writer architecture is not the survey's framing.

title: A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of Large Language Model based Agents
authors: Zeyu Zhang, Xiaohe Bo, Chen Ma, Rui Li, Xu Chen, Quanyu Dai, Jieming Zhu, Zhenhua Dong, Ji-Rong Wen
summary: Systematic survey of memory in LLM agents; method source for the ledger/replay design — shows deterministic append-only logs are a distinctive rather than standard memory choice.

title: Project Sid: Many-agent simulations toward AI civilization
authors: Altera.AL (Robert Yang et al.)
summary: 10-1000+ LLM agents in Minecraft with PIANO architecture show emergent specialization and cultural transmission; large agent societies already exist as research artifacts, though as observed simulations rather than a scaffolded literacy curriculum for a human player.

title: Talk Less, Call Right: Enhancing Role-Play LLM Agents with Automatic Prompt Optimization and Role Prompting
authors: Saksorn Ruangtanusak, Pittawat Taveekitworachai, Kunat Pipatanakul
summary: Tool-augmented role-play NPCs where in-character dialogue and function calls are distinct channels with hard-enforced calling constraints; closest engineering neighbor to C2's split, but optimizes believability/call accuracy rather than making a sovereign writer a governance and literacy principle.

title: Codified Finite-state Machines for Role-playing
authors: Letian Peng, Yupeng Hou, Kun Zhou, Jingbo Shang
summary: Compiles character profiles into codified FSMs so a deterministic symbolic structure tracks latent state while the LLM generates surface dialogue; 2026 evidence that pairing generative expression with a deterministic substrate is an active direction — though its FSM governs character state, not world mutation under player-admission authority.

title: Language as Reality: A Co-Creative Storytelling Game Experience in 1001 Nights using Generative AI
authors: Yuqian Sun, Zhouyi Li, Ke Fang, Chang Hee Lee, Ali Asadipour
summary: AI-native game where LLM-driven storytelling only mutates the world through a narrow deterministic keyword gate; published precedent for rule-gated conversion of LLM output into game state — the gate there is a keyword trigger, not an epistemic verdict-plus-player-admission pipeline.

title: Symbolically Scaffolded Play: Designing Role-Sensitive Prompts for Generative NPC Dialogue
authors: Vanessa Figueiredo et al.
summary: Within-subjects study (N=10) showing role-dependent effects of constraint scaffolds on NPC dialogue; supports the stance that where the constraint boundary is drawn around generative NPCs materially shapes player experience, and shows the evaluation methods Goblin Warren's claims will be measured against.

title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development
authors: Chen Qian, Wei Liu, Hongzhang Liu, Nuo Chen, Yufan Dang, et al.
summary: Virtual software company of role-specialized LLM agents collaborating through structured dialogue phases; the canonical 'agent company/team' system grounding the Superteam scale.

title: MetaGPT: Meta Programming for A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework
authors: Sirui Hong, Mingchen Zhuge, Jonathan Chen, Xiawu Zheng, Yuheng Cheng, Ceyao Zhang, et al.
summary: Encodes SOPs into prompt sequences so role-assigned agents verify intermediate results; its core argument — free generative chatter disciplined by structured, verifiable handoffs — is the industrial-scale analog of C2's separation.

title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
authors: Qingyun Wu, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, Erkang Zhu, Li Jiang, et al.
summary: Framework for conversing agents mixing LLMs, tools, and human input; its human-proxy-agent pattern is the framework-level precedent for the paper's human-gated admission loop.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Model Society
authors: Guohao Li, Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud, Hani Itani, Dmitrii Khizbullin, Bernard Ghanem
summary: Role-playing framework with inception prompting founding the study of LLM 'agent societies'; grounds the Superteam scale as a real research object, not a toy.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, et al.
summary: First empirically grounded taxonomy of multi-agent failures (14 modes across specification, inter-agent misalignment, verification); strong support for C4's claim that agent output is a signal requiring independent verification and gated permission.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox (ToolEmu)
authors: Yangjun Ruan, Honghua Dong, Andrew Wang, Silviu Pitis, Yongchao Zhou, Jimmy Ba, Yann Dubois, Chris J. Maddison, Tatsunori Hashimoto
summary: LM-emulated sandbox letting risky agent tool-use be tested without touching the real world; directly supports letting agents 'express' actions in a consequence-free layer while a separate mechanism controls real mutation.

title: Large Language Model based Multi-Agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges
authors: Taicheng Guo, Xiuying Chen, Yaqi Wang, Ruidi Chang, Shichao Pei, Nitesh V. Chawla, Olaf Wiest, Xiangliang Zhang
summary: Peer-reviewed field map of LLM multi-agent systems; documents that no surveyed system is a playable pedagogy for humans, which helps the novelty argument.

title: How we built our multi-agent research system
authors: Anthropic engineering team
summary: Production orchestrator-worker account (lead agent, parallel subagents, synthesis, ~15x token cost, coordination failure modes); the concrete industrial pattern the Superteam scale renders playable.

title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies (MASS)
authors: Han Zhou, Xingchen Wan, Ruoxi Sun, Hamid Palangi, Shariq Iqbal, Ivan Vulic, Anna Korhonen, Sercan O. Arik
summary: Treats MAS design as search over prompts and workflow topologies; the 2025 structural vocabulary (who talks to whom, in what shape) the Superteam level asks players to internalize.

title: What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations
authors: Duri Long, Brian Magerko
summary: Synthesizes 17 AI-literacy competencies and 15 design considerations; competencies focus on ML basics and critical evaluation, not agentic architecture (proposal/permission/orchestration), leaving the space Goblin Warren targets open.

title: Assessing Implicit Computational Thinking in Zoombinis Puzzle Gameplay
authors: Elizabeth Rowe, Jodi Asbell-Clarke, et al. (TERC EdGE)
summary: Detectors of implicit computational-thinking practices in gameplay correlating with external CT measures; canonical evidence that abstract concepts can be learned implicitly through mechanics — the transfer mechanism C3 hypothesizes and a method source for measuring it.

title: Mindstorms: Children, Computers, and Powerful Ideas
authors: Seymour Papert
summary: Foundational constructionism: powerful ideas are best learned inside microworlds where the concept is embodied in the manipulable environment ('objects-to-think-with'); directly supports the premise that a playable microworld can install a mental model of agent architecture.

title: The Role of Tutoring in Problem Solving
authors: David Wood, Jerome S. Bruner, Gail Ross
venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17, 89-100
summary: Origin of the scaffolding construct: add one extra operation at a time to what the learner can already do; legitimates C3's one-new-gesture-per-level design and C1's staged mental models.

title: What Video Games Have to Teach Us About Learning and Literacy
authors: James Paul Gee
summary: 36 learning principles embodied in well-designed games (regime of competence, probing cycles, situated meaning); supports games as vehicle for a new literacy and gives vocabulary for why gesture-level mechanics can carry conceptual content.

title: Unplugged Activities in the Context of AI
authors: Annabel Lindner, Stefan Seegerer, Ralf Romeike
summary: AI Unplugged hands-on activities for core AI ideas; representative of embodied AI-literacy pedagogy that stops at ML fundamentals, not agentic architecture or governance.

title: Day of AI: Free K-12 AI Literacy Curriculum
authors: MIT RAISE (Cynthia Breazeal's initiative)
venue: MIT RAISE / MIT Open Learning (ongoing to 2026)
summary: K-12 curriculum aligned to UNESCO AI competencies used by 670,000+ students; state-of-practice benchmark whose curriculum-and-worksheet format (not a coherent playable world with progressive mental models) contextualizes what CLAIM-MAIN adds.

title: Fostering students' AI literacy development through educational games: AI knowledge, affective and cognitive engagement
authors: Davy Tsz Kit Ng et al.
summary: TreasureIsland study finding game mechanics and scaffolding improved AI knowledge and engagement; demonstrates efficacy of game-based AI literacy while remaining at ML-concept level, not agent orchestration.

title: Nemobot: Crafting Strategic Gaming LLM Agents for K-12 AI Education
authors: Yuchen Wang, Shangxin Guo, Lin Ling, Chee Wei Tan
summary: K-12 students construct and iteratively improve LLM-based game agents through strategic gameplay; the closest existing work to teaching agent concepts through play — a partial novelty threat to CLAIM-MAIN — but it teaches single-agent construction and prompting, not orchestration scales, sovereign-writer separation, or epistemic governance.

title: Using Games to Learn How Large Language Models Work
authors: Allison Chen, Isabella Pu
summary: Two games teaching how LLMs train and generate token-by-token; confirms games are the active frontier for LLM literacy but targets model mechanics, not agentic architecture.

title: Fostering AI Literacy Through Strategic Play: A Competitive Pathfinding Game for Middle School
authors: Claire Aguiar, Dan Carpenter, Jessica Vandenberg, Wookhee Min, Veronica Catete, Bradford Mott
summary: Classroom study (n=40) where editing a shared grid to observe algorithmic behavior teaches AI concepts; methodologically adjacent to C3's discriminate/regulate mechanics while remaining at classical-algorithm level.

title: A Model for Types and Levels of Human Interaction with Automation
authors: Raja Parasuraman, Thomas B. Sheridan, Christopher D. Wickens
venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics — Part A, 30(3), 286-297
summary: Canonical levels-of-automation framework establishing that machine authority is a design decision decomposable by function, not a monolith.

title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
authors: John D. Lee, Katrina A. See
summary: Seminal trust-calibration model: appropriate reliance requires trust matched to actual capability; the theoretical ancestor of the paper's signal != proof distinction.

title: Some Observations on Mental Models
authors: Donald A. Norman
venue: In Gentner & Stevens (Eds.), Mental Models, Lawrence Erlbaum, pp. 7-14
summary: Foundational statement that users' mental models are incomplete, unstable, and superstitious yet drive prediction; grounds agent literacy as a mental-model formation problem requiring deliberate scaffolding.

title: Mental Models of AI Agents in a Cooperative Game Setting
authors: Katy Ilonka Gero, Zahra Ashktorab, Casey Dugan, et al.
summary: Players with better estimates of an AI agent's abilities won a cooperative game more often, with behavior analysis driving model formation; directly validates games as an instrument for shaping and measuring mental models of AI agents.

title: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance
authors: Gagan Bansal, Besmira Nushi, Ece Kamar, Walter S. Lasecki, Daniel S. Weld, Eric Horvitz
summary: Human-AI team performance depends on the human's mental model of the AI's error boundary, not just accuracy; supports that knowing when to admit an agent's output is a distinct, trainable skill.

title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
authors: Saleema Amershi, Dan Weld, Mihaela Vorvoreanu, Adam Fourney, Besmira Nushi, et al.
summary: 18 validated design guidelines for AI-infused systems; addresses making a single system legible in situ, whereas the paper claims a curriculum that builds the user's model across scales — a positioning gap.

title: Legibility and Predictability of Robot Motion
authors: Anca D. Dragan, Kenton C.T. Lee, Siddhartha S. Srinivasa
summary: Formalizes legibility as distinct from predictability; method source for designing agent behavior channels so expressive output stays readable while world-changing action stays constrained and predictable.

title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
authors: K. J. Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald, Amy X. Zhang
venue: Knight First Amendment Institute working paper / arXiv:2506.12469
summary: Five escalating levels of agent autonomy defined by the user's role (operator to observer), arguing autonomy is a design decision separable from capability; the closest recent framework staging the user's relationship to agents — conceptual/regulatory rather than playable, but it partially anticipates C1's staged progression and C4's authority separation.

title: Exploring Human-AI Collaboration Using Mental Models of Early Adopters of Multi-Agent Generative AI Tools
authors: Suchismita Naik, Austin L. Toombs, Amanda Snellinger, Scott Saponas, Amanda K. Hall
summary: Interview study of 13 developers modeling multi-agent tools as 'teams' of specialized agents; mental models of agent teams are already being empirically characterized — though descriptively for experts, not as a designed progression for lay users.

title: A Systematic Review on Fostering Appropriate Trust in Human-AI Interaction
authors: Siddharth Mehrotra, Chadha Degachi, Oleksandra Vereschak, Catholijn M. Jonker, Myrthe L. Tielman
summary: Systematic review of appropriate-trust methods; shows the field pursues appropriate reliance through in-interface cues rather than playable, structural separation of signal, proof, permission, and authority.

title: Robust Composition: Towards a Unified Approach to Access Control and Concurrency Control
authors: Mark S. Miller
summary: Founds the object-capability model and POLA; draws a formal permission-vs-authority distinction — a direct ancestor of the signal/proof/permission/authority ladder in C4.

title: The Protection of Information in Computer Systems
authors: Jerome H. Saltzer, Michael D. Schroeder
summary: Canonical secure-design principles (least privilege, separation of privilege); the 50-year-old roots of C2's single-sovereign-writer discipline, to be cited as inherited primitives, not novelty.

title: A Comparison of Commercial and Military Computer Security Policies
authors: David D. Clark, David R. Wilson
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (Oakland)
summary: Clark-Wilson integrity model: well-formed transactions and separation of duty (certifier != executor). Goblin Warren's HAL-judges/player-admits rule and single mutating function are a playable Clark-Wilson instance — the mechanism is 1987 prior art, though its use as a pedagogical game mechanic is not.

title: The Dual LLM pattern for building AI assistants that can resist prompt injection
authors: Simon Willison
summary: Proposes a privileged LLM that acts but never reads untrusted content and a quarantined LLM that reads but cannot act; the closest architectural prior art to C2 — LLM output as untrusted input that must never directly drive privileged action predates the paper by three years.

title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
authors: Kai Greshake, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, Mario Fritz
summary: First systematic treatment of indirect prompt injection; establishes the threat model motivating C2 — generative and retrieved text are attacker-influenced signals, never trusted commands — and gives C4's signal-vs-authority distinction adversarial grounding.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
authors: Edoardo Debenedetti, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes, Nicholas Carlini, Daniel Fabian, Christoph Kern, Chongyang Shi, Andreas Terzis, Florian Tramèr
summary: Protective system layer ensuring untrusted retrieved data can never alter program flow, with capability-based data-flow controls; the 2025 state of the art for exactly the C2 property in a production security setting — the paper's residual novelty must live in the pedagogical setting.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
authors: Luca Beurer-Kellner, Beat Buesser, Ana-Maria Creţu, Edoardo Debenedetti, et al.
venue: arXiv:2506.08837 (ETH Zurich, Google, Microsoft, IBM consortium)
summary: Catalogs six principled patterns (action-selector, plan-then-execute, dual-LLM, etc.); lets the article honestly frame its governance loop as a playable member of a now-named pattern family rather than a new invention.

title: C2PA Technical Specification (Content Credentials), version 2.x
authors: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (Adobe, Microsoft, BBC, Intel, Truepic, Sony, Google, OpenAI, Meta, et al.)
venue: C2PA / Linux Foundation JDF standard (founded 2021; spec 2.4 current)
summary: Industry standard for signed, tamper-evident provenance manifests; the real-world receipts infrastructure the game's every-state-change-writes-a-ledger-event invariant dramatizes — provenance as evidence about history, distinct from permission or authority to act.

title: Event Sourcing
authors: Martin Fowler
venue: martinfowler.com (with CQRS as named by Greg Young, QCon SF 2006)
summary: Canonical event-sourcing description: state as a replayable derived view over an event sequence, with CQRS separating command from query path; the direct engineering ancestor of the Warren's append-only ledger, replayEvents(), and derived views — a known pattern being repurposed pedagogically.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human Oversight
authors: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
venue: Official Journal of the European Union
summary: Requires high-risk AI systems be designed for effective human oversight, including the power to disregard, override, or halt; the strongest institutional warrant that AI output is recommendation, not authority — which both legitimizes the game's model and shows the concept is established policy rather than a new proposal.

title: Hearing Gesture: How Our Hands Help Us Think
authors: Susan Goldin-Meadow
summary: Canonical synthesis of two decades of evidence that gesture is not decorative but cognitive: gesture-speech mismatches index readiness to learn, and gesturing itself helps learners think, remember, and acquire new concepts. This is the foundational anchor a learning-sciences reviewer will expect behind any gesture-design hypothesis; it grounds C3's premise that hand actions can carry conceptual load distinct from verbal/symbolic channels.

title: Where the Action Is: The Foundations of Embodied Interaction
authors: Paul Dourish
summary: The HCI-side foundation for embodied interaction: meaning in interactive systems arises from situated, physical-social engagement rather than abstract symbol manipulation. Positions Goblin Warren's gesture-per-level interface as embodied interaction in Dourish's sense, and lends conceptual support to C2's separation of expressive engagement from the deterministic system core (interaction as meaning-making layered over computational mechanism).

title: The Mathematical Imagery Trainer: From Embodied Interaction to Conceptual Learning
authors: Mark Howison, Dragan Trninic, Daniel Reinholz, Dor Abrahamson
summary: Exemplar of embodied design: students learn proportionality by moving two hands to keep a screen green, constructing 'attentional anchors' that later become formalizable mathematical objects. Demonstrates the design pattern C3 relies on — assign a motor-control task whose solution structure IS the target concept — and is the method template for designing L0-L2 gestures whose kinesthetic structure mirrors agentic-AI concepts (e.g., regulate/temporize as continuous control).

title: Emboldened by Embodiment: Six Precepts for Research on Embodied Learning and Mixed Reality
authors: Robb Lindgren, Mina C. Johnson-Glenberg
summary: Field-defining precepts for pairing embodied-learning theory with gesture-input technologies; argues body activity catalyzes learning but that embodied-tech research has been technology-driven and under-theorized. Gives C3 both its warrant (gesture input can generate learning) and its burden (a gesture hypothesis must specify the concept-to-action mapping and be evaluable) — useful for framing C3 explicitly as a testable design hypothesis rather than a claim of demonstrated efficacy.

title: Do Gestural Interfaces Promote Thinking? Embodied Interaction: Congruent Gestures and Direct Touch Promote Performance in Math
authors: Ayelet Segal (advised by John B. Black)
summary: Establishes 'gestural conceptual mapping': touchscreen gestures improve learning only when congruent with the cognitive structure of the task (tapping for discrete counting, dragging for continuous magnitude). This is the mechanism C3 presupposes — that WHICH gesture is bound to WHICH concept matters — and it directly supports the per-level differentiation (drag/hold vs. catch/discriminate vs. turn/regulate) while implying C3 must justify each gesture-concept congruence, not just gesture use per se.

title: Embodied Science and Mixed Reality: How Gesture and Motion Capture Affect Physics Education
authors: Mina C. Johnson-Glenberg, Colleen Megowan-Romanowicz
summary: Empirical evidence that gesture/motion-capture manipulations produce measurable gains on abstract science concepts (electric fields), with level of embodiment and active generativity predicting learning. Answers the reviewer question 'has gesture-to-abstract-concept transfer actually been demonstrated?' affirmatively — supporting C3's plausibility while setting the evidentiary bar C3 has not yet met (Goblin Warren has design rationale, not transfer data).

title: Artificial Intelligence Education for Young Children: A Case Study of Technology-Enhanced Embodied Learning
authors: Weipeng Yang, Xinyun Hu, Ibrahim H. Yeter, Jiahong Su, Yuqin Yang, John Chi-Kin Lee
summary: Kindergarten case study (Hong Kong, 6-week intervention) showing young children can learn AI concepts through embodied interaction with intelligent agents. Proves the intersection 'embodied learning x AI literacy' is already occupied, so Goblin Warren cannot claim to be the first embodied approach to AI education — but it targets generic AI concepts in early childhood, with no designed gesture vocabulary and no agentic/governance content, leaving C3's specific contribution intact.

title: AI Unplugged: Embodied Interactions for AI Literacy in Higher Education
authors: Reddig et al. (Georgia Tech TAIL lab)
venue: EAAI-26 (AAAI Symposium on Educational Advances in Artificial Intelligence); arXiv:2602.13242
summary: Recent work explicitly using embodied, unplugged interactions (role-play, physical activity) to teach AI concepts to higher-ed learners — the closest published neighbor to C3. It demonstrates embodied AI-literacy pedagogy but via unplugged role-play rather than an in-game, level-indexed gesture vocabulary, and does not address agentic multi-agent governance or a scale progression; C3 must be positioned relative to it rather than claiming the embodied-AI-literacy space outright.

title: A Meta-Analysis of the Cognitive and Motivational Effects of Serious Games
authors: Pieter Wouters, Christof van Nimwegen, Herre van Oostendorp, Erik D. van der Spek
summary: Meta-analysis of 77 learning studies (N=5,547) and 31 motivation studies (N=2,216): serious games beat conventional instruction on learning (d=0.29) and retention (d=0.36) but not motivation (d=0.26, ns). Effects are moderated: games work best over multiple sessions and when supplemented with other instruction — directly usable to defend (and appropriately hedge) the implied transfer premise of CLAIM-MAIN.

title: Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors: Douglas B. Clark, Emily E. Tanner-Smith, Stephen S. Killingsworth
summary: K-16 meta-analysis: digital games significantly enhanced learning vs. non-game conditions (g=0.33, k=57), and value-added comparisons show that DESIGN decisions within a game (not the medium itself) drive learning gains. The design-over-medium finding is the strongest available warrant for arguing that Goblin Warren's specific mechanics (gesture staging, governance loop) are what matters, not 'gamification' generically.

title: Computer Games in Education
authors: Richard E. Mayer
summary: Evidence review distinguishing three genres of game-learning research (value-added, cognitive-consequences, media-comparison) and insisting claims for educational games be grounded in evidence-based learning theory. Provides the methodological vocabulary the paper should use to state what kind of learning claim CLAIM-MAIN is making, and a warning against overclaiming from visionary rhetoric.

title: Video Game Training Does Not Enhance Cognitive Ability: A Comprehensive Meta-Analytic Investigation
authors: Giovanni Sala, K. Semir Tatlidil, Fernand Gobet
summary: Three meta-analytic models (k=310/315/359) find small-to-null effects of video game training on general cognitive ability; far transfer from games is close to zero against active controls. This is the adversarial source the paper must pre-empt: it does not touch domain-specific content learning (Wouters/Clark territory) but it kills any reading of CLAIM-MAIN as 'playing the game makes you generally better at reasoning about AI' absent taught domain content.

title: A Game Design Vocabulary: Exploring the Foundational Principles Behind Good Game Design
authors: Anna Anthropy, Naomi Clark
summary: Canonical verbs-and-objects vocabulary: games are built from verbs (player actions) whose meaning is taught through resistance, feedback, and level design rather than explicit tutorials; 'teach and reinforce rules wherever and whenever we have the opportunity.' Direct method source for framing C3's one-gesture-per-level hypothesis as verb introduction and layering.

title: How I Got My Mom to Play Through Plants vs. Zombies (GDC 2012 talk; 10 tutorial tips)
authors: George Fan
venue: Game Developers Conference (GDC Vault; summarized at Game Developer)
summary: The PvZ designer's tutorial doctrine: spread mechanic teaching across the whole game, teach one thing at a time, let players learn by doing (level 1 teaches 'plants shoot right, zombies walk left' hands-on), make the tutorial invisible, and encode function in visual form. This is practitioner precedent for exactly the one-gesture-per-level staging of C3, from a game that onboarded strategy-genre novices.

title: The Impact of Tutorials on Games of Varying Complexity
authors: Erik Andersen, Eleanor O'Rourke, Yun-En Liu, Richard Snider, Jeff Lowdermilk, David Truong, Seth Cooper, Zoran Popovic
summary: Multivariate study of 45,000+ players across eight tutorial designs in three games: tutorials raised play time up to 29% in the most complex game but gave no significant engagement gain in simpler games whose mechanics are discoverable by experimentation. Empirical nuance for C3: gesture staging should scale with mechanic complexity (L0's drag/hold may need no explicit instruction; L2's regulate/temporize verbs justify heavier scaffolding).

title: Design Club: Portal — A Detailed Analysis of the Tutorial Mechanics in Portal
authors: Dan Emmons, Daniel Floyd (Extra Credits Design Club; summary at Laughing Squid)
summary: Analysis of Portal's onboarding: sequential test chambers teach one simple system at a time, then layer complexity by combining mechanics; environmental Isotype icons, dotted connector lines, and color-coded state replace text prompts, and the full portal-gun verb set is only granted after ~20-30 minutes of staged play. The standard-reference worked example for incremental verb introduction backing C3, and its diegetic signaling of world state is a useful analogue for C4's playable governance signals.

title: Intelligence Rising: A Strategic Simulation of AI Futures
authors: Shahar Avin, Ross Gruetzemacher, et al. (Cambridge CSER / Oxford / Wichita State)
venue: Intelligence Rising / Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (facilitated scenario role-play exercise)
summary: The best-known playable AI-governance exercise: a facilitated strategic role-play where participants embody state officials and AI-lab executives navigating AI race dynamics over simulated decades. It is a policy/foresight wargame for adult decision-makers, not a videogame, and it teaches geopolitical race dynamics rather than hands-on agent orchestration or admission-gating mechanics.

title: Strategic Insights from Simulation Gaming of AI Race Dynamics
authors: Ross Gruetzemacher, Shahar Avin, James Fox, Alexander K. Saeri
summary: Peer-reviewed analysis of 43 Intelligence Rising sessions, extracting strategic lessons (destabilizing race dynamics, value of cooperation, corporate-state misalignment). Establishes that AI-governance simulation gaming is an active academic research method with published outcome analysis — Goblin Warren must cite this lineage and position itself as a different genre (single-player mechanical literacy game, not multi-stakeholder scenario exercise).

title: Performance or Governance? Serious Game and Workshop as a Tool for Fostering Awareness of Responsible AI
summary: A CHI 2025 serious game where teams allocate compute and human resources (engineers, ethics experts, safety experts) trading off AI performance against trust/governance. Proof that 'playable AI governance for awareness' already exists in HCI literature — but it is a resource-allocation workshop game about organizational responsibility, with no admission-gate mechanic, no gesture vocabulary, and no separation of generative expression from deterministic mutation.

title: The Oversight Game: Learning to Cooperatively Balance an AI Agent's Safety and Autonomy
authors: William Overman, Mohsen Bayati
venue: arXiv:2510.26752 (Stanford GSB working paper; rev. Feb 2026)
summary: Formalizes human-in-the-loop oversight as a two-player Markov game: agent chooses play/ask, human chooses trust/oversee, with an alignment guarantee under Markov Potential Game conditions. 'Game' here means game theory, not a playable artifact — but it is the closest formal neighbor to C4's admit/hold/deny gate and must be cited to show C4's contribution is experiential/epistemic (players feel signal-vs-permission) rather than a new formal control result.

title: Empowering Learners for the Age of AI: AI Literacy Framework for Primary and Secondary Education (AILit)
authors: OECD and European Commission (with CodeAI)
venue: OECD / European Commission joint framework, published 17 June 2026
summary: The flagship institutional AI-literacy framework: 19 competences in four domains — Engage with AI, Create with AI, Manage AI, Shape AI. The 'Manage AI' domain gestures at oversight but the framework (per available descriptions) does not codify agent-orchestration or admission-gating competencies as distinct skills, leaving the gap Goblin Warren's three-scale progression targets; the paper should map its levels onto AILit domains rather than claim no framework exists.

title: Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named
authors: (arXiv:2605.27396 authors)
summary: A 2026 position paper that already codifies principal-side agentic competencies: delegation (what authority you grant), oversight (monitoring/constraining agents), accountability attribution, attack-surface awareness, agent-specific informed consent, and calibrated trust. This is the strongest single threat in this domain: the *prose codification* of orchestration/governance competencies exists, so CLAIM-MAIN cannot be 'first to identify agentic-AI literacy competencies' — it must be the first *playable operationalization* of them.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
authors: Paul F. Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom B. Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei
venue: NeurIPS (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30)
summary: Foundational human-in-the-loop work: humans compare trajectory pairs to train a reward model that shapes agent behavior (the root of RLHF). Key contrast for C4: human feedback here is a *training signal* that diffuses into the policy, whereas Goblin Warren's admission gate makes human judgment a *runtime permission* that alone mutates the world — the paper should use this to sharpen signal-vs-permission.

title: Safely Interruptible Agents
authors: Laurent Orseau, Stuart Armstrong
venue: UAI 2016 (Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence)
summary: Canonical corrigibility-adjacent result: constructs RL agents (e.g., modified Q-learning) that neither resist nor game repeated human interruption, building on Soares et al.'s 'Corrigibility'. Anchors the HITL/corrigibility neighborhood for C4: the ML literature asks how to make agents *accept* the override; Goblin Warren asks how to make humans *competent at wielding* it — complementary, not overlapping.

title: $800 'AI' robot for kids bites the dust along with its maker
authors: The Register staff (Thomas Claburn)
summary: Reports the December 2024 shutdown of Embodied Inc and the bricking of Moxie robots, drawing explicit lessons about cloud-dependent AI companions: the child-facing pet had no local autonomy or user-side authority, so the vendor's collapse terminated the relationship. Moxie's pedagogy was social-emotional development, never governance-of-AI content — its death is a governance failure the product never taught about.

title: Closing FAQs – Moxie Robot (incl. OpenMoxie open-sourcing effort)
authors: Embodied Inc
summary: Embodied's own closure notice confirming Moxie's core functions required continuous connection to company cloud servers, no refunds, and a promised community-driven 'OpenMoxie' fallback for basic offline functionality. Primary evidence that the leading pedagogically-framed AI pet located all authority in vendor infrastructure — the exact signal/permission/authority conflation the paper's C4 ladder names.

title: Loona Smart Robot Dog — AI Pet & Interactive Companion (ChatGPT-4o powered, Blockly coding for kids)
authors: KEYi Technology
summary: Commercial petbot marketed for kids 5+ with an explicit educational framing: STEM/coding via Google Blockly in the companion app, plus ChatGPT-4o conversation, gesture control, and home monitoring. Its pedagogy is programming the pet, not governing an agent — no admission gates, no expression/mutation separation, no authority concepts surface as content.

title: Moflin: AI Companion and Robot Pet
authors: Casio Computer Co.
summary: Casio's plush emotional-AI pet that 'learns and responds uniquely' to its owner and grows an evolving simulated emotional state. Makes no pedagogical or governance claim whatsoever — pure companionship — and so anchors the far end of the product spectrum against which the paper's governance-as-content Pet scale is novel.

title: Taking Bold Steps to Keep Teen Users Safe on Character.AI (removal of open-ended chat for under-18s)
authors: Character.AI
summary: Character.AI's October–November 2025 announcement removing open-ended companion chat for minors, adding age assurance (in-house model plus Persona) and Parental Insights, under lawsuit and regulator pressure. Governance here is operator- and parent-imposed wrapper around the companion; the user never learns or exercises governance concepts through the experience itself.

title: AI Toys are NOT Safe for Kids — Advisory (150+ expert/org signatories incl. Sherry Turkle, Jenny Radesky)
authors: Fairplay for Kids
summary: Field-defining November 2025 advisory warning parents against LLM-era AI toys (naming Miko, Loona Petbot, Gabbo/Curio and others): manufactured trust, privacy invasion, displacement of human play. Frames the entire commercial pet/companion category as ungoverned chatbot wrappers — evidence that no product in the category treats governance literacy as its content, which is the gap the paper's Pet scale claims.

title: Principles of Safe AI Companions for Youth: Parent and Expert Perspectives
authors: (arXiv preprint authors, 2510.11185)
summary: Academic study eliciting parent and expert principles for safe youth AI companions (transparency, disclosure of AI status, data practices, parental oversight). Confirms that even the research frontier treats safety/governance as external constraints and design requirements on companions — not as concepts the child learns by operating governance mechanics — leaving the paper's experiential-governance claim intact.

title: Epistemological Problems of Testimony (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Nick Leonard (current edition; earlier editions by Jonathan Adler)
summary: Canonical survey of the reductionism vs. anti-reductionism debate about testimonial justification, covering Coady's (1992) anti-reductionist critique, Lackey's dualist repair of the divide, and Goldberg's reliabilist anti-reductionism. Single citation that certifies the C4 ladder's ancestry claim: whether a hearer's acceptance of another agent's say-so needs independent positive reasons (reduction to perception/memory/inference) or carries default warrant is a century-old structured debate, so grading the epistemic force of an agent's output is not an ad hoc move.

title: Learning from Words: Testimony as a Source of Knowledge
authors: Jennifer Lackey
summary: Lackey argues the reductionism/anti-reductionism dichotomy is non-exhaustive: positive reasons on the hearer's side are necessary but not sufficient for testimonial warrant (dualism), and — crucially for AI — testimonial knowledge flows from the reliability of the *statement*, not the speaker's own knowledge. Her statement-reliability view is the standard bridge cited by the machine-testimony literature for why outputs of non-knowing sources can still transmit warrant; it directly underwrites C4's separation of the signal rung from the proof rung.

title: Monitoring and Anti-Reductionism in the Epistemology of Testimony
authors: Sanford C. Goldberg (with David Henderson)
summary: Defends anti-reductionism against the objection that hearers' counterfactual sensitivity to defeaters (monitoring) collapses it into reductionism: default entitlement to accept testimony coexists with an obligation to filter. Goldberg's monitoring-plus-default-entitlement structure is the closest classical analogue to Goblin Warren's gate mechanics — acceptance is gated, not automatic, yet the gate is not a full re-derivation of the claim — giving C4's permission rung (accept-without-proving, but only through a filter) a named philosophical precedent.

title: How to Do Things with Words
authors: J. L. Austin
venue: Harvard University Press / Oxford (posthumous William James Lectures, 1955)
summary: Origin of the performative/constative distinction, the locutionary/illocutionary/perlocutionary triad, felicity conditions, and *uptake*: an utterance only achieves its illocutionary force when the right conventional procedure and hearer uptake are in place. This is the ladder's speech-act ancestry for the top rungs — permission and authority are felicity-conditioned statuses conferred by an institutional procedure (in the game, the player's admission act), not properties of the utterance's content. Searle's later taxonomy of illocutionary points (verified in the same results) extends this and can be co-cited.

title: Can Artificial Entities Assert?
authors: Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller
venue: The Oxford Handbook of Assertion (Oxford University Press)
summary: Introduces *quasi-testimony*: machine outputs that phenomenologically resemble testimony and conform to a norm parasitic on the testimonial norm of the context, without the machine being a full assertor. This is the field's first canonical intermediate-status category for AI outputs and the nearest single precedent to C4 — it shows the 'grade the status, don't binarize it' move already exists, but it defines only one intermediate stratum on the epistemic side and says nothing about permission or authority conferral.

title: Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion
authors: Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne
summary: Evaluates the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion against proxy-assertion and fictionalist accounts, rejects both, and proposes *proto-assertion* — a graded, developmental category for LLM outputs at the edge of full illocutionary status. Together with quasi-testimony this confirms that 2024-era philosophy grades AI-output status along the assertion dimension; it strengthens the ladder's respectability while marking exactly where C4 must claim less (intermediate epistemic statuses exist) and more (nobody stacks them into a four-rung epistemic-to-deontic ladder with mechanical gates).

title: Experts or Authorities? The Strange Case of the Presumed Epistemic Superiority of Artificial Intelligence Systems
authors: Andrea Ferrario, Alessandro Facchini, Alberto Termine (authorship from prior knowledge; title/venue/year verified in search result)
summary: Part of the 2024-25 debate (with the 'Epistemic Deference to AI' / AI Preemptionism literature surfaced in the same results) on whether reliable AI systems are Artificial Epistemic Authorities whose outputs preempt a user's own reasons, in Zagzebski's sense. Argues the expert/authority distinction is illegitimately collapsed for AI: reliability grounds at most expertise, while authority is a normative relation requiring accountability and reason-responsiveness. This is precisely C4's signal-vs-authority gap argued independently in professional philosophy, and supports the game's rule that authority is never derivable from output quality — only conferrable by the admitting human.
